content:
Most construction projects don't fail during construction.

They fail before the first shovel hits the ground.

They fail at the moment the owner chose the wrong general contractor.

Florida has over 40,000 licensed contractors. Choosing between them — when they all have websites, all claim 30+ years of experience, and all promise they'll deliver on time and on budget — is one of the hardest decisions you'll make.

Here's the framework we use at Keentel General Contractors. Not to sell you on us. To help you make the right call — whoever that ends up being.

The contractor you choose will have more impact on your project's success than any other single decision you make.

First, Understand What a GC Actually Does

This sounds obvious. It isn't. A general contractor doesn't just build things. A GC is the central coordinator of a complex, multi-party project. On any given commercial build, they're managing:

  • Architects and engineers who designed the project
  • Subcontractors across electrical, plumbing, HVAC, concrete, framing, and finishing
  • Material suppliers, deliveries, and procurement timelines
  • Municipal permitting offices and building inspectors
  • Your budget, your schedule, and your expectations

When all of that works together, you barely notice the GC. The project just happens. When it doesn't, you notice. Loudly.

The GC is the conductor. The building is the music. You'll know immediately whether they know what they're doing.

The 8 Things That Actually Matter

1. Are They Licensed in Florida?

Non-negotiable. Full stop. In Florida, general contractors must hold a license issued by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR). You can verify any license at myfloridalicense.com in 60 seconds.

If they're not licensed — walk away. Not run. Walk, calmly, and never look back.

Verify here → myfloridalicense.com — search by name or license number before you sign anything.

2. Do They Carry the Right Insurance?

Two types. Both required.

  • General Liability Insurance — protects your property if something goes wrong on the job
  • Workers' Compensation Insurance — protects you if a worker is injured on your site

Ask for certificates. Not promises. Certificates. Any reputable contractor hands these over without hesitation. Hesitation is your answer.

3. Have They Done This Before — Specifically?

Experience matters. But relevant experience matters more. A contractor who builds warehouses across Hillsborough County may not be the right choice for a restaurant buildout in downtown Tampa. Different codes. Different sequencing. Different coordination requirements.

Ask specifically: "Can you show me three completed projects similar to mine?" If they can't — that's your answer.

At Keentel → We deliver pre-construction, design-build, general construction, commercial remodeling, residential remodeling, emergency restoration, and electrical contracting across Florida. If your project type is in our portfolio, we'll show you the proof.

4. Will You Talk to Their Previous Clients?

References aren't a formality. They're intelligence. Don't just collect names. Call them. Ask three questions:

  • Did they finish on time?
  • Did the final cost match what was quoted?
  • How did they handle problems when they came up?

The third question is the one that matters most. Problems happen on every project. The quality of the contractor is revealed in how they respond — not in whether problems occur.

5. Do They Have a Real Process?

Gut instinct is not a project management system. Ask them: How do you manage schedule? How do you communicate with clients? What's your change order process? How do you select and vet subcontractors?

Vague answers mean vague execution. A contractor with a documented process — pre-construction planning, weekly reporting, milestone reviews, change order protocols — has built projects before. They've learned what goes wrong. They've built systems around it.

You don't want a contractor who improvises. You want one who has seen your problem before and already knows the solution.

6. What Does Their Communication Look Like Right Now?

This is the most underrated signal in the selection process. How quickly did they respond to your first inquiry? Were they clear in their proposal? Did they follow up when they said they would?

The way a contractor communicates during the bidding phase is a direct preview of how they'll communicate during your project. Slow, vague, or inconsistent communication now means slow, vague, or inconsistent communication when something goes wrong on your job site.

Communication is not a soft skill in construction. It's the skill.

7. Are They Financially Stable?

This one most owners never ask about. It's one of the most important. A contractor in financial trouble will prioritize cash flow over your project. They'll delay subcontractor payments — creating lien risk on your property. They'll cut corners on materials. In the worst case, they'll abandon the project entirely.

Ask how long they've been in business. Ask about their bonding capacity. A performance bond means an insurance company has vetted their financial stability and will back the project if the contractor defaults.

Florida Red Flag → A contractor who asks for more than 10% upfront, or who can't explain their payment structure clearly, is managing their cash flow with your money. Walk away.

8. Is the Price Honest?

The lowest bid is not the best bid. A low bid can mean missing scope. Underestimated labor. Cheap materials. A contractor who plans to make up the difference through change orders once you're committed.

The highest bid isn't automatically better either. It might mean inefficiency, padded margins, or overkill on spec. The right bid is a detailed, itemized proposal that clearly shows what's included and what isn't — from a contractor who can defend every line.

Compare the scope, not just the number.

Florida-Specific Factors Most People Miss

Florida isn't a generic construction market. It has specific requirements that matter when choosing a GC.

Florida Building Code Compliance

The Florida Building Code is one of the most stringent in the country. Hurricane-resistant construction requirements, energy efficiency standards, wind load specifications — these aren't optional and they vary by county.

Your GC must know them cold. Not generally. Specifically, for Hillsborough County, for Miami-Dade, for Orange County, for wherever your project is.

Local Permitting Knowledge

Permitting timelines in Florida municipalities vary enormously. Tampa's permitting process is different from Orlando's. Sarasota moves differently than Jacksonville.

A contractor who works regularly in your county knows the local permit reviewers, the common sticking points, and how to structure applications to minimize back-and-forth. That knowledge is worth months on your schedule.

Storm Season Planning

If your project runs June through November, storm season is a schedule variable. An experienced Florida GC builds this into the plan. They don't discover it mid-project.

Subcontractor Relationships

Florida's active construction market means good subcontractors are in demand. A GC with established, long-term subcontractor relationships gets priority scheduling. A GC without them scrambles — and scrambling shows up in your schedule and your quality.

The Questions to Ask in Every Interview

Bring these to every contractor meeting. The answers will tell you everything you need to know.

  • "Walk me through a recent project that went off-plan. What happened and how did you handle it?"
  • "Who will be my direct point of contact throughout the project?"
  • "What's your process for managing subcontractors on-site?"
  • "How do you handle material procurement and long-lead items?"
  • "What's included in your proposal that your competitors typically exclude?"
  • "What's the most common thing that causes your projects to go over budget — and how do you prevent it?"

You're not just evaluating answers. You're evaluating how they think. A contractor who answers these questions confidently, specifically, and honestly is showing you how they'll manage your project.

Red Flags That Should End the Conversation

Some things are disqualifiers. Not concerns — disqualifiers.

  • No license or an expired license
  • Can't provide insurance certificates immediately
  • Discourages you from pulling permits — "it'll take too long"
  • Asks for full payment or large deposit upfront
  • Refuses to provide references or references are evasive
  • No written contract — "we work on handshakes around here"
  • Bid is dramatically lower than every other proposal with no explanation
  • Slow to respond or hard to reach during the bidding phase

The Rule → If something feels wrong during the selection process, it will feel worse during construction. Trust that instinct. There are 40,000 licensed contractors in Florida. Move on.

Why the Right Decision Pays for Itself

A professional general contractor costs money. That's true. Here's what else is true.

A GC who delivers your project on schedule saves you months of lease payments, carrying costs, or revenue you couldn't generate in an unoccupied space. A GC who delivers your project on budget saves you the overruns that routinely reach 15–30% of project cost on poorly managed jobs. A GC who manages subcontractors properly saves you from lien disputes, rework, and the legal costs of contractor failures.

The GC's fee is not a cost. It's an investment in the probability that your project succeeds.

You don't hire a surgeon because they're the cheapest option. You hire them because you want the outcome. Construction is the same.

faqs.q: How many bids should I get for a construction project in Florida?
faqs.a: Three is the standard. Enough to understand the market and compare approaches — not so many that the process becomes unmanageable. What matters more than the number of bids is ensuring every contractor is pricing the exact same scope of work. A bid comparison only means something if the bids are comparable.

faqs.q: What licenses should a general contractor have in Florida?
faqs.a: At minimum, a Florida Certified General Contractor license issued by the DBPR. Depending on the scope, they may also need specialty licenses (electrical, plumbing, mechanical). You can verify any license at myfloridalicense.com. Always check before you sign.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a general contractor and a subcontractor?
faqs.a: A general contractor manages the entire project and holds the primary contract with you, the owner. Subcontractors are specialists — electricians, plumbers, concrete crews — who are hired by and answer to the GC. You have one relationship: with the GC. They manage everyone else.

faqs.q: Should I hire a local Florida contractor or a national firm?
faqs.a: For most projects in Florida, a local contractor has meaningful advantages: knowledge of local permitting, established relationships with Florida subcontractors, accountability through their local reputation, and familiarity with Florida Building Code requirements county by county. National firms make sense for highly specialized projects or those requiring resources beyond local capacity.

faqs.q: What should be in a Florida construction contract?
faqs.a: Every Florida construction contract should include: detailed scope of work, project timeline with milestones, payment schedule tied to progress (not arbitrary dates), change order process and authorization requirements, insurance requirements for contractor and subs, warranty terms, and dispute resolution process. Never begin work without a fully executed written contract.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a construction permit in Florida?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on the municipality and project type. Simple residential permits in responsive jurisdictions can issue in 1–2 weeks. Complex commercial projects in high-volume departments may take 2–6 months. A GC who works regularly in your county will have realistic timelines and the relationships to manage the process efficiently.
